money_at_stake.rationale: The occurrence's own thesis (hyperscaler AI capex supercycle) is now a same-year, board-approved number, not a projection: the four largest US hyperscalers are on track for roughly $725bn in combined 2026 capital expenditure, up about 77% from around $410bn in 2025. That clears GT_100B by a wide margin on its own, before counting the additional capex from Oracle and other neoclouds the same reporting cycle attributes to the same buildout. Not reduced to a lower band for the uncertainty in the aggregation: even the most conservative company-level figures the source gives (Amazon ~$200bn, Microsoft ~$190bn, Google $175-205bn, Meta $125-145bn) sum well past $100bn on their own. This leg previously carried a second corroborating item (CNBC, "$700 billion" headline figure); on 2026-08-30 that URL returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch and the Wayback Machine was unreachable from this environment, so the item is deleted rather than repaired with a substitute source. The remaining item alone still supports the band with room to spare.

Both are listed on US exchanges with public tickers. Scored below the prior run's 85 for two reasons. First, a third corroborating item (Eaton, Pulse2 coverage) is deleted on this pass: on fetch, the 240% data-center order figure it cited did not appear anywhere on the page, the 42% Electrical Americas figure it cited does not match the page's own 41%, and the page's own August 2 publication date points to Q2 2026 results rather than the Q1 2026 framing the item used, so the whole item was unsupported rather than partially supported. Second, with the pool now resting on two names instead of three, part of it still runs outside clean listed capture: the generation link is only EMERGING per the existing chain map (data/chains/ai-infrastructure.json), some of the fastest power fixes route through regulated utilities and private EPC/interconnection work, and a share of equipment demand still flows through diversified conglomerates where AI is one growth line among several.

capture_odds.rationale: Two of the same named listed suppliers that carry the public_reach evidence show sustained margin expansion driven partly by price, not only by volume, which is the direct test for whether this money sticks as profit rather than getting competed away. Vertiv's own investor-relations release states an adjusted operating margin of 20.8% for the first quarter, up 430 basis points year over year, driven by operational leverage on higher volume and positive price-cost, inclusive of tariff impacts and associated tariff mitigation countermeasures: margin expanding while absorbing tariff cost pressure is a pricing-power signal, not a pure volume story. GE Vernova's Electrification segment, the same segment the deleted SEC citation had targeted, shows the same pattern at larger scale, now sourced to a reachable secondary report of the company's own Q2 earnings materials rather than the unreachable filing: orders of $6.3 billion running at approximately 1.7 times revenue, segment EBITDA more than doubling from $314 million to $671 million as margin expanded 700 basis points to 18.4%, and segment backlog nearly doubling to $44.6 billion from $27.1 billion. A book-to-bill above 1.7x alongside 700 basis points of margin expansion means demand is outrunning delivered capacity at rising, not falling, margin, which is the signature of a supply-constrained market rather than a price-taking one. Scored 70, short of the 85-plus anchor (concentrated, qualification-locked, pricing power visible), because both citations show margin expansion riding alongside volume growth and neither states a qualification-lock, sole-source, or long-term-contract mechanism explaining why competitors also selling into this same buildout (Schneider Electric, Eaton, Siemens Energy, Hitachi Energy, nVent) could not eventually compete the margin back down; the evidence supports real, current capture without confirming its durability. Well above the 40 anchor (some specs, mostly price-taker), since a price-taker in an oversupplied market does not expand margin by hundreds of basis points while its own backlog nearly doubles.

timing_fit.rationale: The money is moving inside the occurrence's own window, not projected past it: anchor_date is 2023-01-01 with a stated window running to the late 2020s, and 2026 hyperscaler capex is already realized, board-approved spend (money_at_stake leg), not a forecast. GE Vernova's data-center orders had already more than doubled 2025's full-year total by Q2 2026, on a $176bn total backlog, which is a near-dated conversion signal on the same timeline. Scored below the prior run's 85 because the item that gave this leg a second, more granular near-term data point, Vertiv's backlog framed as a 12-to-18 month delivery window, is deleted on this pass: the cited TIKR article confirms the $15bn backlog of binding purchase orders but contains no sentence stating a 12-to-18 month window, and the Motley Fool article used elsewhere in this file for the same backlog also does not state that window verbatim, so the figure is unconfirmed at any source this appraisal has fetched. Not scored at the very top anchor for the same reason as before: the largest single fix on the generation side of this same chain, new nuclear and SMR capacity, lands mostly in the 2030s per this signal card's own cited evidence (only 9.8GW of committed nuclear capacity, 80.4% not yet in commercial operation as of mid-2026), so a real share of the full chain's spend sits past the horizon this appraisal is scored against even though the equipment-and-grid spend does not.
